blocks.text: Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry that gives the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation. With the mole, Avogadro's number, molar mass, molar volume and molar concentration, quantitative relationships between reactants and products can be established from balanced equations. Six types of relationship can be studied: mole-mole, mass-mass, volume-volume, mole-mass, mole-volume and mass-volume. To use them, the information hidden in a balanced equation must be read. For N2(g) + 3H2(g) gives 2NH3(g): one mole of N2 reacts with three moles of H2 to form two moles of NH3; one molecule of N2 reacts with three molecules of H2 to form two molecules of NH3; 22.4 dm3 of N2 reacts with 67.2 dm3 of H2 to form 44.8 dm3 of NH3; and 28.0 g of N2 reacts with 6 g of H2 to form 34.0 g of NH3.

blocks.title: Keep in mind
blocks.text: Stoichiometric calculations assume that all the reactants are completely converted into products, that the laws of conservation of mass and definite proportions are obeyed, and that no side reaction occurs.

items: Start from the mass of a known solid, the volume of a known gas, or the molar concentration of a known solution.
Calculate the number of moles of the known using the relevant formula.
Find the ratio of the known and the unknown reactant or product from the balanced equation.
Calculate the number of moles of the unknown using that ratio.
Convert the moles of the unknown to mass, volume or concentration.

blocks.alt: Left: the equation N2 + 3H2 = 2NH3 read four ways, in moles, molecules, volumes at STP and masses, with a box of three assumptions. Right: five stacked boxes joined by arrows, from the known quantity, to its moles, to the mole ratio, to the moles of the unknown, to the final mass, volume or concentration.
blocks.caption: Reading a balanced equation and the five steps of a stoichiometric calculation (original diagram after the printed approach).
blocks.long_description: One balanced equation gives mole, molecule, volume and mass relationships at once, and mass is conserved: 28.0 g plus 6.0 g gives 34.0 g. Every calculation follows the same path: turn the known quantity into moles, multiply by the coefficient ratio from the equation to get the moles of the unknown, and turn those moles back into the quantity wanted. The three assumptions, complete conversion, the two laws, and no side reactions, underlie all of it.
